speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to join the other Members of the House in congratulating the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt), who, a short time ago, delivered her maiden speech in this House. I am sure that she will be a credit not only to her constituents but an asset to this House of Commons.
I listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) last Thursday, Mr. Speaker, when he opened debate on this Bill.
At Page 20400 of Hansard the Minister said:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-134 is an Act respecting rebate of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act and is a piece of legislation which is extremely important to the farm community and to all Canadians.
A little later, as reported on the same page, he said:
This measure will help to assure the survival of many Canadian farmers who are presently facing serious financial difficulties.
Like the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) who spoke before me, I, too, read the report in the November 4, 1982, issue of the Globe and Mail. The effect was rather shocking, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to put a portion of that report on the record. It refers to a conference called by the United Grain Growers in Banff. The conclusion the conference reached was this:
Only good yields and high deliveries of grain will prevent an even steeper drop in income-
The article went on to say:
Farmers' incomes will drop 36 per cent in Saskatchewan and 34 per cent in Manitoba. In Alberta, improved livestock prices will cushion the blow and income will drop 15 per cent.
In the country as a whole, they are predicting that there will be a drop in farm income of 28 per cent over 1981.
Farmers in Canada are facing more than serious financial difficulties, Mr. Speaker; many are facing bankruptcy. The bankruptcy rate in the farming population is up by some 65 per cent. If the trend continues, the result will be a tragic one for the whole farming community. Grain and livestock prices have fallen. If one examines the statistics, one finds that the
total farm debt is between $18 billion and $20 billion. The interest that farmers pay on that debt is in the neighbourhood of $3 billion. We should put that $3 billion in perspective, Mr. Speaker.
If we go back to the estimates we will see that in 1968-69, the total budget for the whole of the Dominion of Canada- that is, the money it took to operate the Government of Canada-was $10.8 billion. This year, the farmers of Canada will spend almost one-third of that amount on interest payments to service their debt.
To put that in even better perspective, if we examine the records of Canada, we will find that the cost of servicing the country's debt in 1968 was $1.5 billion. That was for the entire debt of Canada in 1968. Today, farmers pay double that amount to service their debt. That is a catastrophe created by the Liberal Government opposite, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Agriculture-who, incidentally, is not in the House, Mr. Speaker-will undoubtedly recall that he was in Moose Jaw earlier this year to attend a meeting called by a group of livestock producers who found themselves in terrible financial difficulty. The market was low and interest rates high, and they were facing bankruptcy. The Minister arrived late, but I was there for eight hours. I listened to the livestock producers and to many grain producers who spoke at that meeting. They pointed out the disastrous effects the high interest rates were having on their industry. I am sure that farmers in other parts of the country have told the Minister the same thing.
In response, the Minister introduced this Bill, which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture says will only help 500 farmers. There are 320,000 farmers in Canada but this Bill will only help 500 of them. Yet the Minister of Agriculture pats himself on the back for that.
The Minister has allowed the Farm Credit Corporation to go to the American market to borrow $100 million in bonds. It is interesting to read the analysis of this borrowing which was given by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) when he spoke in the House on November 4. He used 12 per cent as a basic rate on this $100 million borrowed on the American market. This appears to be a fair rate. He pointed out that the Canadian dollar stands at 82.5 cents compared to the U.S. dollar, which would add another 2 per cent to the interest rate. Of course, because of the fluctuation in the foreign exchange market, the Farm Credit Corporation will have to hedge against changes in the currency market. He estimated this at another 2 per cent. Another 1 per cent must be added for the administrative charges incurred by the Farm Credit Corporation in making the loans. I do not complain about that 1 per cent, because I think the Farm Credit Corporation is to be commended for keeping the cost of servicing loans to the farmers down to 1 per cent.
When we add the 12 per cent, the 2 per cent because of the Canadian dollar being at 82.5 cents, the 2 per cent for hedging and the 1 per cent for administration, then the Farm Credit Corporation will have to charge an effective interest rate of 17
November 8, 1982

per cent. It would appear, then that when the farmer borrows this money he will be tied in for ten years to an interest rate of 17 per cent. That is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker.
On March 30, 1982 this House passed Bill C-88 which made changes in the Farm Credit Corporation. We were very pleased about that on this side. In Clause 8 of the Bill, Section 13 of the Farm Credit Act was changed, the new Section 13.(1) reads as follows:
The Corporation may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, borrow money by any means,-
I emphasize that phrase "by any means", Mr. Speaker.
-including issuing and selling bonds, debentures, notes and other evidences of indebtedness of the Corporation.
We were pleased because it said, "Borrow money by any means". For quite a long time we on this side of the House were making proposals such as the agribond, a scheme to assit farmers who were called upon to pay large capital gains tax. We felt that the change brought in by the Bill back in March would allow the Government to bring in the innovative ideas which we had suggested. As I said, we had made these suggestions for some considerable time.
I read the Minister's speech of last Thursday, the Minister never gives credit where credit is due. As reported on page 20400 of Hansard, he said:
-using the agribond principle that was not originally thought up by those opposite, Mr. Speaker, but was brought up and talked about by people for many years-
If the principle has been around for many years, why has the Minister or the Governent not made use of it? Is it because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has no clout with his Cabinet colleagues? Can he not sell them on a good idea? Does he prefer to borrow money on the international market? Does he not really give a damn for the failing agricultural economy? Is he perhaps afraid of financial institutions? What kind of a Minister of Agriculture is he?
When 1 spoke in the House in February on the FCC Bill, the one which allowed the Corporation to borrow money by any means, I talked about borrowing money from the Farm Credit Corporation at the then rate of 16.75 per cent. I used the example of farm land selling at $1,000 an acre. It is not uncommon in western Canada to have farm land sell at $1,000 per acre and up. Generally speaking, farmers use a two-year crop rotation. They summer fallow one year and they crop the next; half and half. In other words, a farmer crops half his acreage each year. If we take $1,000 per acre land, with a two-year crop rotation and $6 wheat, the farmer has to produce 50 bushels per acre to pay the interest alone. On top of that, of course, he has to add his seed, municipal taxes, fertilizer, the price of gas and oil, his repairs and depreciation. He just cannot survive.
With the scheme at which the FCC is looking, as approved by the Minister, it will cost the borrower of American money 17 per cent. If we use the same figures of $1,000 an acre and a
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
two-year crop rotation, with grain at $4.75 per bushel compared with $6-and the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board says that farmers this year will get the initial payment of only $4.75 per bushel-with interest at 17 per cent, it will require 71 bushels per acre to pay the interest alone. If one were fortunate enough to buy land at $500 per acre, it would require 36 bushels an acre to pay the interest. Farmers, grain producers and livestock producers just cannot survive. That is what the Government has been doing and what it is doing in borrowing $100 million from the United States. It will put farmers further and further in debt and possibly into bankruptcy.
For many years farmers in western Canada have been concerned about the capital gains tax. It is a substantial tax. Many farmers are afraid to retire because of the enormous amount of tax they would have to pay. People might say that since they are selling their land for substantial amounts they should be able to pay capital gains tax, but generally speaking the only money farmers have on which to retire is the proceeds from the sale of their farms.
In the last two or three elections Members of the Liberal Party in their campaign in western Canada said that they would do something about capital gains tax. They did not say they would eliminate it, but I recall the Liberal candidate in Assiniboia saying at a press conference in Regina that if they were elected they would update valuation day. Hollow promises; nothing was ever done. There was no change in the capital gains tax. In fact, what did they do? In the June budget of about a year ago they eliminated the income averaging annuity, one means by which a retiring farmer was able to alleviate the burden of capital gains tax. This is what the Government thinks of farmers.
When I spoke in the House in February of this year on the amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act, I talked about a method of helping farmers with capital gains tax, helping the FCC with cheaper money and helping the borrowers with lower interest rates. It was not the first time I had spoken about it; I had spoken about it in public meetings before. I suggested that we should allow a farmer who was retiring or selling out and was faced with a substantial capital gains tax to invest the capital gains in the FCC and also allow him to invest the proceeds on the sale of his inventory. There is a heavy tax burden when a farmer sells out and has an inventory of grain. There is also a substantial tax burden when he sells his equipment because of capital gains.
1 suggested that we could allow the retiring farmer to invest the money from these three sources in the FCC on the condition that, if he invested the money for a period of five years, the capital gains tax would be waived. The money that he invested would draw interest at 8 per cent, as I suggested in February. It may or may not be taxable because the farmer would be using this as his retirement income in the five-year period. I suggest that the 8 per cent that he receives for that five years should not be taxable. However, if it were to be taxed, it would be to the extent that the 8 per cent exceeded the average bank rate.

November 8, 1982

I am sure that if such a program was introduced coupled with the agribond concept, there would be a great deal of money available to the Farm Credit Corporation for lending purposes. If the Farm Credit Corporation could obtain that money at 8 per cent and take into account its administration charges of 1 per cent, it could lend the money to the borrower at 9 per cent instead of the 17 per cent it will have to charge for money that it will have borrowed on the American market. A program such as I have suggested would allow the young farmer to begin farming. It would allow the struggling farmer to survive and would prevent the appreciation in value of farm lands.	*
There is no question that the capital gains tax has effectively increased the value of farm lands because on many occasions farmers who are selling their farms have come into my constituency office inquiring what their capital gains tax will be. I have asked them, since they do have accountants, why they would want to know other than for income tax purposes. They have told me quite frankly that they will add the cost of the capital gains tax on to the sale price of the land. In effect, capital gains tax has caused an appreciation in farm land which makes it difficult for the young farmer, or any farmer, to purchase land.
If the Minister of Agriculture were to adopt a scheme such as I have suggested, he could be very popular. Apparently he is more interested in helping the foreign market and the large financial institutions than he is in helping agriculture. I believe the banks have proven that they are capable of looking after their own affairs. I believe the insurance and investment companies have proven that they can look after themselves. The Minister has indicated that the credit unions were concerned about the agribonds or the scheme which I have suggested to alleviate capital gains. I suggest that the effect of Canada Savings Bonds sales at high interest rates has a greater effect on credit unions than a proposal such as ours.
As said by the ITon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), this would be a self-help program because the farmers would be helping each other to survive. This is an important point, because if the agricultural sector does not prosper, the other sectors of our economy cannot prosper.
In closing, I urge the Minister to consider seriously our proposals. If he believes in the agricultural industry he will attempt to sell those suggestions to the cabinet.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to join other Hon. Members in congratulating the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt) on making her first speech in the House. I know that we do not often speak to many Members in this institution when we rise, but there is something about the institution, as there should be, which makes that first speech a major undertaking. The Hon. Member did a masterful job and I look forward to hearing more speeches of that quality from her in this institution.
The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) spoke eloquently about some proposals that should certainly be considered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We have a more depressing outlook for agriculture today than we have
had for many decades. I would like to discuss world trade and what it means to the income of the agricultural producers. Before doing so, I would also point out that many farmers in Canada today are looking at the future of agriculture with some reservation.
I have represented the riding of Wetaskiwin for ten years. In that time I cannot remember any farmer coming to me and wondering about their future. They have always indicated that while their year was not as productive as anticipated, the future was bright. However, they are now coming to me to ask whether they should continue to incur further debts to stay in agriculture or if they ought to sell. However, the prospect of selling their farm does not look very bright either because the price of land has decreased in value. The state of our economy has affected the price of land all across Canada. When farmers look to auction sales for removal of their equipment, they are finding that that picture does not look very bright either because the price of tractors, combines and cultivation equipment has also decreased greatly because farmers cannot afford to buy that inventory. If you have money at this time, particularly in western Canada, there are many bargains to be found at auction sales.
If the banks call their loans and farmers are forced to sell their land or equipment, they are then faced with capital gains tax. They cannot even take the revenue from that land and equipment to pay off their debts because they have to pay the Government a capital gains tax.
It is no wonder that we have heard many eloquent speeches during the last few days on this subject of credit. Credit is a very important instrument to the agricultural industry. We cannot exist today without it. When my father took the farm over from my grandfather, he lost his crops to nature three years in a row. He was able to survive, however, because the debts that he had incurred were not large. At that time fertilizer and chemical sprays were not necessary because the land was sufficiently productive. I know a very few farms today in my constituency that can survive one crop loss. Farmers today obtain loans simply to sow their crops. Farmers do not have enough money in their savings just to put their crops in the ground, and that is true of the farm I am running as well. Until about five years ago we had sufficient funds to put our crops in each year from what we were able to earn from our sales. However, this year, last year and the year before that, we had to borrow money to put the crop in. This year, myself and many other farmers in my constituency are wondering if we need to finance the operation alone, because we are not receiving enough return from revenue to pay that debt off. The future does not look too bright.
The Bill will help about 500 farmers. The budget offered a $50 million program involving special financial farm assistance loans, which helped 382 farmers. Our experts are telling us that 20,000 farmers in this country are in distress today. These
November 8, 1982

two Bills are helping 880 of those. That is good, but what about the others?
Day after day we are told of the increasing numbers of bankruptcies. There has been a 65 per cent increase this year over last year. Unless we get the incomes of the farmers up or their costs down, it is sad to say but we will be facing more bankruptcies.
The current level of interest rates is one of the largest factors, but another is the cost of production which is also undergoing a dramatic increase. As we know, people who produce machinery, fertilizer and so forth must pay higher labour costs. They must pay higher input costs for the production of that equipment which they pass on to the farmer and he, in turn, must pay more. Costs of production are rising year after year. This year, we on the Prairies found that the price of grain decreased. The price of a bushel of barley delivered to the elevator is 31 cents less than last year. The price of wheat, as was just enunciated by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw, has gone from $6 a bushel down to $4.75 a bushel. We are asking that our farmers be able to continue to operate as their incomes drop and their costs rise. I do not know how we expect them to go on for very long. Statistics show that they cannot go on for very long.
We have a desperate problem involving one industry in this nation which must be addressed. Excellent ideas have been put forward as to how we can address the problem. This Bill will help only a few. Our party is supporting it, but we must have policies to address the longer term problem. How can we do that? We must do more than bring Bills to the House, as the Minister constantly does. We debated one in February this year, we are debating one now and certain Bills have been brought forward from the budget, all dealing with credit and how we can give farmers more loans or rebates of interest on loans. There have been no initiatives which would assist farmers to bring down their costs or, conversely, to raise the price of their commodities. There are ways of doing that, even in these hard times.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) refer to the area of energy. I join with him because I also feel there is an ability to lower costs, in the energy field. One of the most important ways, one which we could adopt tomorrow, would be to lower the tax taken on gasoline and diesel fuel by the federal Government, some 40 cents per gallon on diesel and 60 cents a gallon on gasoline. The Province of Alberta has led the way by removing its provincial sales tax on gasoline. We applaud that action because it has assisted farmers in my Province a great deal. We are big users of energy. Farmers are large users of energy. When tax is removed, it has an immediate beneficial effect on their bank account and on their ability to pay interest rates and input costs. The Government should follow that example. The removal of the tax would have immediate effects. It should not only be removed from a gallon or a litre of diesel fuel or gasoline, but it should also be extended, until we rise out of this difficult period of time, to those products derived
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
from natural gas and oil, such as sprays and fertilizers, which constitute input costs.
I have some statistics. For every dollar per barrel increase in the Canadian price of oil, the price of nitrogen fertilizer increases by $5.88 per tonne. Hydrous ammonia increased by $10.54 per tonne and ammonium phosphate increased by $4.75 a tonne. All these are essential in the production of crops today. The price of pesticides and weed sprays per gallon is 87 cents. In the year to which I have been referring, the price of commodities has dropped, but the price of oil has risen by $2.75 a barrel and the federal take in tax on that oil is some 40 cents to 60 cents. Therefore, there would be some immediate effect in cutting farmers' costs if we lowered the federal tax on gasoline and diesel fuel and lowered input costs, such as those I have mentioned.
The other way would be to promote the use of renewable energy. The Government could do that if it put its mind to it. I will not repeat the speech of the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, but he referred to the use of alcohol. Farms have the capacity to produce alcohol from stills in a very efficient manner and the Government ought to be sending out information on how farmers can build such stills which would make it very simple to produce one's own fuel.
People in Nova Scotia, I believe, have invented an excellent straw-burning grain dryer which we have read about in our papers and magazines. Why should we not buy the patent and send it out to farmers across the nation so that they can cut their costs of drying grain by building or having this type of furnace built? These are the kind of ideas the federal Government could use. In my brother's house we have installed the first heat pump in Canada which uses the ground as its source of heat. It has been working excellently in the last two months, heating the house from the heat that is down in the ground, at a cost much less than natural gas or diesel fuel. We also have wind energy and biomass. Any livestock producer has the capacity to produce fuel from his livestock's own waste material. All these are available, but we are not getting the information out to the farmers who are hungry for it.
Another way of increasing the price of commodities is through the Canadian Wheat Board. Most of us were astonished when we heard that this crop year the Government and the Canadian Wheat Board would allow the initial price to the farmers to drop, given what I have just said about the rise in input costs. It is within the realm of the Canadian Wheat Board to keep the initial price at the level it was last year. It has the ability to borrow money from the federal Government to foot the bill. To my way of thinking, it would be much better for us to put public funds through that mechanism to keep the price at the level it should be, rather than to bring it in through the back door in the way this Bill is attempting, so that all farmers could have the benefit. The price should be kept the same. We should not allow it to drop and cause the loss of decades of work as farmers go bankrupt. No one can understand that unless he has experienced it or watches as his constituents come in and bare their souls as they look toward

November 8, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
losing their farms this week, next week or a month from now, with no chance to stop it from happening.
1 see some Hon. Members opposite, some Hon. Members in the NDP and some Hon. Members in the Conservative Party. In the last four years they have been talking with their American counterparts because farmers in the United States are having the same difficulties as farmers in Canada in so far as meeting their balance of payments is concerned. We asked them why we compete so well with one another that we actually sell our grain below the cost of production. What a ridiculous situation. The United States is the only country with a major surplus of food in the world today. That is the principal reason why the price of grain is as low as it is. Another reason is that many countries in the world simply cannot afford to pay for food. However, there are many other countries to whom we deliver grain that can afford to pay and should be paying more. Both U.S. and Canadian representatives agree that we should not be selling grain below the cost of production since we sell 75 per cent of the surplus grain in the world. We also agree that our costs of production are very similar. It would be simple to work out a formula.
Canadian Members of Parliament together with Senators and Congressmen in the United States can and must take a hold of this problem because our Ministers and officials are not. We must work out solutions and the formulae so that we will not compete with one another at a cost below that of production. Once world prices rise above the cost production, there is no problem; we should compete and we should compete well with one another. However, as it is now we are simply hurting our own farmers by doing what we are.
The last report was delivered to the Minister eight or nine months ago. It was well received by him. He said it contained good ideas. Departmental officials have been meeting for a number of years. Perhaps they are caught up in simple language in some kind of international agreement, but while they agree on the principle, they have been unable to put anything together that could be brought forward to our respective institutions.
A few months ago farmers in western Canada met with farmers from the United States. They agreed that the principle was sound and asked why it could not proceed. Yet nothing has yet been put together. I think it is time now for that to be done. We will be seeking from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board a meeting with Senators and Congressmen so they can iron out these problems. We should put as much pressure as we can on the Minister here and the Secretary in the United States to get together and agree not to sell grain and oilseeds below the cost of production.
Countries like Japan, the Soviet Union, those in the European Community, China and many of the Arab countries who buy grain from us can afford to pay the cost of production, and they should be paying it. In fact, some of these countries add on so many dollars per bushel so as not to compete with their
own farmers. In some countries the amount is as high as $6 a bushel. This is added on in the form of a tariff. This is money which our farmers could desperately use at the moment. If the income were ever to get so large that farmers were making an extraordinary profit it could perhaps be put into an account to assist those countries who cannot afford to pay and whose people are starving. In this way we could get their cost down. This is an excellent program. It has been talked about and legislators in both countries agree that it is time for action.
Let me point out that there are other ways of lowering costs. Canada has one of the best agricultural research capacities in the world. Excellent material is being produced month after month. Surely within that material there are ways that farmers can cut their costs. We should ask our very capable scientists to put these ways together. This material should be distributed to our farmers so they can use whatever part of it is pertinent. We should not do what was done in February when the Department issued a report. In it we found such things as "How can you get by in distressed times?" Some of the suggestions were absolutely unbelievable. They could only emanate from a Department. Other suggestions included: "Sell off some unproductive land". Most farmers are using every acre they have in the most productive way possible. How can they choose which corner to sell off? We also find these words: "You can always work off the farm". There are some farmers who have the time to do that. Most of them are working for every hour possible that they have off the farm. But that does not work all that well because the Government only allows $2,500 of income to be earned off the farm before it is taxed at the rate of 40 per cent or 50 per cent. Again, that solution is not a total solution, but it was not a bad suggestion.
Another suggestion was to raise livestock-hogs or cattle- in unused buildings. That was done years ago when provincial Governments encouraged farmers to get into the livestock business. They were even given loans. Most farmers were in bankruptcy the following year because they got into another area of production that did not raise the kinds of funds necessary to meet expenses, particularly when farmers were taking up loans to buy breeding stock and to fix up old buildings. Those kinds of suggestions are not adequate. We have to ask our experts, which we have in abundance, to search their records and come up with suggestions. The Department of Agriculture should then get the suggestions out to farmers so they can decide whether or not they fit into their operations.
Then there is the suggestion of improving our lending institutions and capabilities. The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw talked about that. His was an excellent suggestion on capital gains. I will not repeat it because he did such a good job of explanation.
What about the Small Business Development Bond? That concept was brought forward by us when we were in Government. This program is now being snowed under with red tape and a bureaucratic maze which results in its being of hardly any use to the farmer in need. In most cases the bank will not accept the individual as a credit risk. If the individual is
November 8, 1982

accepted, he has to go through so many procedures that he is almost bankrupt before he can get the bond. Such questions as: "Can you sell off any land? Do you have any relatives from whom you can borrow money? Is there some other way by which you can rearrange your finances?" are asked. As my colleague says, they should buy a Loto Canada ticket. These questions are asked before one is accepted as an applicant for a Small Business Development Bond.
However, that is a concept on which you can build. It is an excellent concept. It has helped some farmers in Canada. We should eliminate many of the roadblocks that are put in the way of the Small Business Development Bond.
We have the agribond concept, about which much has been spoken in this debate. We have heard of examples in other countries. Members have talked particularly about those that are offered in the United States. We can get ideas from the Federal Land Bank Association, the Production Credit Association, the Farmers Home Administration and the Commodity Credit Association. All of these ideas could fit into the Canadian realm of agriculture and would be better than some of the situations that farmers face now.
Finally, there is transportation and shipping. We are making moves in that area. We are making sales. The Minister of Agriculture could be helping this country. We have had the Canagrex Bill before us for quite some time. The Minister is too bull-headed to recognize that if he removed the sections that are distasteful to farmers and left in the sections which promote and facilitate exports, that Bill could be passed and we could be using it to help farmers get more sales in livestock, grains and horticultural products. But no, he persists. As a result, the Bill is held up.
There is a need to facilitate the sale of agricultural commodities throughout the world. We have embassies and institutions around the world, but they have only limited expertise in agriculture. We should send people there who know how to sell our agricultural commodities. This would assist our farmers.
We have had, put many statistics on the record today and last Thursday that I am sure the farmers do not like to hear. I am not going to repeat very many of them. However, some of the statistics are astonishing to me and I am sure to people across this country, such as the amount of debt. In the United States, and the situation is not much different in Canada, net farm income in 1982 is estimated at $18 billion. Total farm debt is approximately $200 billion. At 10 per cent interest, that is $20 billion being paid in interest. That is right off the net farm income. That statistic is readily available.
I tried to find the comparable statistics for Canada. It is surprising how close they are. Total Canadian farm debt is $18 billion. Net farm income is $4.9 billion and the gross is $18 billion. One can see that the debt is equal to the amount of money we are capable of generating through agricultural production. How long can that be allowed to continue? As has been stated, we must get the prices of our commodities up to a reasonable level or the costs down.
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
The Farm Credit Corporation has been a major lending institution in Canada for the farmers. At one time it loaned about 70 per cent of the long-term capital in Canada. Any farmer will tell you it is not the long-term debt that will kill him but the short-term debt. In the last few years, many farmers have been incurring a lot of short-term debt in order to replace machinery. They must invest between $50,00 and $100,000 for a new combine and tractor. That is generally short-term debt. At today's interest rates, that debt is too cumbersome for them to handle. We need institutions that will provide farmers with the opportunity to turn their short-term debt into long-term debt at lower interest rates.
Today Farm Credit Corporation loans account for far less than the 70 per cent they once did. These are now down to 25 per cent. We should be looking to the Farm Credit Corporation for other ways to quickly provide long-term debt to farmers at lower interest rates to help them through these desperate times. That is not being done with this Bill. It has not been done through any of the bills which came before us in the last couple of years. We are not assisting in solving very difficult problem.
There is another problem being faced by the Farm Credit Corporation. The amount of capital available and the demand for capital is so great that not all the loans for which the farmers are asking can be made. Therefore, loans are being made to fewer and fewer farmers. In fact, during the first two and a half months of this year they distributed money to 16 per cent fewer farmers than last year, with a larger budget. That is one of the problems this institution is facing.
While this Bill is providing extra money, half of that money is really coming from a reorganization within the Department. As a result, fewer farmers are being helped than was anticipated. It is a bit of a deception and it is not helping the very desperate needs of farmers.
Farmers are facing input costs of unbelievable magnitude. Interest expenses are up by 39 per cent this year over last year, machinery repairs are up by 24 per cent and feed is up by 11 per cent. There is not one area in agriculture not facing these difficulties.
The subject of farm credit has been well covered in the last two days of debate on this Bill. We can only hope that some of the suggestions will be considered. We have asked why the farm fuel tax cannot be removed. We have asked about the agribond and the capital gains concept. Many other suggestions have been made. We want to hear the answers. We have also covered statistics which farmers do not like to hear. We have no other choice than to support this Bill as it has been brought forward. I am glad we have had this debate; it is long overdue. We ought to have many more like it. Perhaps we can get some positive answers, with some changes to the legislation so that we can help the farmers of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR REDUCTION OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
that Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments to inform the House about the Small Business Investment Grants Program, to explain its provisions and the way it is being applied.
I want to begin by saying that the Government of Canada is very much aware of the concerns of the small business community and has sought to promote good relations with this very important sector of Canadian society, and to develop practical solutions to the problems that small businessmen face. That is why we formed a task force to look into the financing of small business in Canada and published the report of that task force in May. The report, which does not contain policy recommendations as such, will nevertheless serve as input for discussion of future options for Government action.
We have also recently formed the Small Business Advisory Committee, which is made up of members of the small business community, lending institutions and academics. This committee will advise the Government on matters concerning small business and suggest policy options. One of the items they will be tackling is the report of the small business financial review.
I also want to inform Members of the House of the fact that in our discussions with the small business community, we have met with a very enthusiastic response to the Government's six and five per cent restraint guidelines. As Members are well aware, one of the problems facing Canada's many small businesses has been high interest rates, which have reduced the entrepreneur's ability to finance capital investment and research and development. Thus the small business community, which the federal Government recognizes is extremely important to the over-all Canadian economy, has been hampered in its ability to generate economic activity and create jobs in this crucial time of worldwide economic recession.
The federal Government has listened to the representations of the small business community, and has recognized this problem. That is why in the June 28 budget of the former Minister of Finance a program was announced which was designed specifically to alleviate the financing problems of
small businesses in today's economy. That program is the Small Business Investments Grants Program. Under the provisions of the program an interest subsidy of up to four percentage points per year is granted to eligible small business borrowers to finance acquisition of new depreciable assets, or to finance research and development. An amount of $400 million was set aside in that budget to be devoted to this program. The interest subsidy will be paid for two years from the date of the loan.
One of the attractive features of the Small Business Investment Grants Program is its simplicity. It has been made available through the lending institutions. In other words, application for a grant is made to the lending institution as part of negotiating a loan in the regular manner. It is the lending institution which processes the application with the Government.
Loans qualifying under the program can be obtained from chartered banks, trust companies, insurance companies, credit unions, Caisses Populaires, the Federal Business Development Bank, the Farm Credit Corporation, any lending agency of the Government of Canada or of a Canadian Province or Territory, as well as any investment company as defined under the Investment Companies Act. This ensures that ready access to the benefits of the program is available to small business anywhere in Canada.
As far as the eligibility of the borrower is concerned, I want to explain that for the purposes of this program small businesses that qualify include corporations that are eligible for the low corporate tax rate for small business, partnerships whose members are all individuals, and proprietorships-and here I want to emphasize that this includes farmers and fishermen. Businesses engaged in a profession, however, do not qualify.
Loans from $10,000 to $500,000 can be subsidized by a small business investment grant. A small business may obtain more than one loan under the program, provided the total borrowings do not exceed the $500,000 upper limit. The interest rate subsidy under the program is up to four percentage points: with the effective interest floor being i2 per cent, so that the 4 per cent grant will be reduced when the grant and any other assistance available would lower the interest rate to less than 12 per cent.
The program was designed as a temporary measure to assist small businesses during this difficult economic period. It therefore applies to loans made between June 29, 1982 and March 31, 1983. And here I should emphasize one point that may possibly have been misunderstood by the business community. Since for obvious reasons it took sometime after the June 28 announcement before the necessary forms and information could be distributed to all the lending institutions, some business people did not become aware of the program until some weeks after June 29. They may have assumed that only future loans would qualify under the program. The fact is,
November 8, 1982

however, that any loan on or after June 29 qualifies, if the criteria I have mentioned are otherwise met. In other words, a business person who arranged a loan in, say, July this year, and only afterwards learned of the Small Business Investment Grants Program, may still apply to his banker for the interest rate subsidy.
In order to ensure effective delivery of this program through the lending institutions, officials have worked very closely with associations such as the Canadian Bankers' Association. I must say that I am grateful to the financial community for the co-operation we have received. Hundreds of thousands of brochures on the program have been taken up by lenders for distribution to borrowers through their local branches, and several major lenders have been promoting the program quite enthusiastically.
In addition, I would like to thank the Hon. Members on both sides of the House for their efforts to promote the program to their constituents. More than 16,000 forms have been distributed so far. Applications are coming in at a rate of 30 or 40 per day. There is every reason to expect that with implementation of our own advertising campaign, along with continuing promotion of the program by the lending institutions, the rate of applications will increase over the coming weeks.
1 will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by repeating that the Small Business Investment Grants Program is a temporary measure, designed to meet a specific need at a specific time. We do not pretend that in itself it meets all the needs of the small business community, and we are continuing to examine ways and means to assist small businesses which constitute such an important part of the Canadian economic scene.
Mir. Chris Speyer (Cambridge): Mr. Speaker, before commencing my remarks, may I take this opportunity to formally convey my best wishes to the Minister on his new portfolio, and to tell him that in anything he does to further the small business community, certainly this Party and this particular critic, will assist.
With respect to the legislation that is before the House, may I say, as I did on June 30, two days after the former Minister of Finance brought down his budget, that this Party, and myself, as the critic for small business, will support anything which we believe is productive for the small business community, and we include this piece of legislation. There will be no obstruction whatsoever. This matter should go through. Unfortunately, though, I believe it is too little, too late, and I intend to expand on that in a few moments.
Let me say at the outset, that statistics in normal prosperous times for the small business person are really abominable. One out of every two businesses which have been in business two years fail. Four out of five business in business for five years fail. That is in normal times and with normal risks. Persons far more intelligent than myself who have done studies say the reason is under-capitalization, mismanagement, or a combination of both. But, in the last two years with interest rates, the magnitude of which I can only call sometimes extortionary, we
Small Business Investment Grants Act
have seen economic carnage among the small business community that words cannot properly emphasize.
Just to give some dimension to the problem, in the first nine months of this year, bankruptcies were up in the business community-and I am talking about businesses as opposed to personal bankruptcies-by 43 per cent over last year, and 66 per cent over two years ago. The frightening aspect of that, Mr. Speaker, is that the number of bankruptcies does not provide the true statistics.
What we are trying to analyze is how many people are going broke. We know since the mid-60s that the vehicle used by people who go broke is no longer bankruptcy. People declare bankruptcy in order to avoid always having to pay a creditor. In other words, they want to extinguish their debt. Bankruptcy legislation is good legislation because it is controlled through the courts of this country and we have the statistics. What people do not recognize, though, is that the normal person goes broke by way of receivership. What happens is that the bank, when it calls its note, moves in on the business under its floating charge debenture. And we do not have any statistics on that except that the insolvency Association of Canada says there are ten businesses that go insolvent for every one that goes bankrupt.
By using our eyes, our ears and all our senses we know the plight of small business in this country. This results not only because of mismanagement or undercapitalization, but because of the harsh reality of interest rates which, when I was going to law school, would have been unconscionable transactions.
These comments come from a riding in southwestern Ontario, the heartland of Canadian manufacturing, or at least we thought it was such. In my community we have gone to an unemployment level of over 20 per cent. A year ago it was approximately 7 per cent. There was one sure thing about Cambridge; people knew that you could always get a job in Cambridge as there were lots of textile mills and shoe factories. But the harsh reality of the last year, the fact that we have 22 per cent unemployment, has caused the citizens of my community to literally go through a nervous breakdown. It is not like ridings in Cape Breton which traditionally have had high unemployment. It is not like ridings in the province from which the Minister comes, which have had to endure unfortunately high unemployment over a period of time. This is something new and it is happening in the heartland of southwestern Ontario. You can believe me, Mr. Speaker, that the emotions in my community over the state of the economy are very difficult to exaggerate by words.
I would like to talk about the personal effect on small business people because I just received by today's mail a letter from a small-businessman who was making running shoes. He was holding back certain Canada Pension and Unemployment Insurance moneys in connection with his workers, and the Department of National Revenue effectively closed him down. The amount of his indebtedness for payroll deductions was

November 8, 1982
Small Business Investment Grants Act
$13,270, and he wanted to make a deal. He could not. Third party notices of garnishee were distributed. In order to do the man justice, I am going to read a letter he sent to the department. He said this:
Our company has been going through some difficult times and it has not been our intention to withhold the payments, but we have not been able to generate enough funds to do more than meet the payroll monies due to our employees. We have survived on a month to month basis hoping that the footwear quotas would be reintroduced. We have fought "tooth and nail" to survive the depression and now that the quotas have been reintroduced the signs are positive as to our recovery. However, it appears the government, through its Kitchener collection office, has determined that their pound of flesh should come before our recovery and before the jobs of our employees.
When the auditor left our business he informed me that we would be contacted by the persons incharged of collections in Kitchener so that an arrangement could be made to try to settle the outstanding amounts. We did not hear from the persons in Kitchener, but received in the mail demands on Third Parties sent to all our customers. I immediately phoned a Mr. Schnurr at Collections in Kitchener and asked him "Why he had not contacted us first?" and informed him that his actions would likely put us out of business.
The bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is that as a result, this company has just recently had to lay off 20 people because of the $13,000. They will be going on Unemployment Insurance. What this small-businessman asked for was time to settle the account. That time was not granted and we have another company that has gone under.
One more very vivid experience, came to my attention within the last few days when I was back in Cambridge. The bank loan of a small business had been called. The person involved is a very solid citizen, one who tried to endure, but could not because of the high interest rates which have affected all western economies, not just Canada's. I certainly acknowledge that. The bank in question called the guarantee of this man's mother and father. I will not mention his name because 1 know he would not want me to cause them embarrassment. His parents are 65 years of age and all they have is a house. His father has a very small pension and a veteran's allowance. Those people are going to have their house taken away.
I know all Members from all sides of the House are hearing similar stories. One almost breaks into tears when the reality of these situations comes across the desk; when you see the person who has to bear this kind of a burden.
High interest rates have really hurt the small-businessman. Unfortunately, the budget policies of the predecessor to the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) caused untold hardships in our country. I believe there is a crisis of faith and of trust in Government. I say that if this Government were to introduce the finest economic policies it could muster, I am not sure the business community would trust it.
When are the rules going to be changed? I hark back to the November budget. I give some credit to the current Minister of Finance because in his recent economic statement I think he clearly undid some of the harm his predecessor did. I think he should be given credit for that. But there are some matters which affect the small business community that have not been changed. I invoke the assistance of the Minister sitting in his
place in the House tonight because the most important thing to assist the small business community is the capital cost allowance. I will refer to Liberal policy in 1972.
In May of 1972 the Hon. John Turner, the then Minister of Finance, brought down a budget. The issue before the country at that time was jobs. There are 33 forms of depreciable property, ranging all the way from 5 per cent to 100 per cent. Because one out of five people are employed in the manufacturing sector, it was determined at that time, that in order to create jobs a speedy write-off would be given under Class 28 of depreciable property. That would mean, for example, that if a businessman, when he had money in his coffers, wanted to purchase some equipment he could write it off in two years. That was an incentive for him to do so.
What has happened so far? Well, the budget of November, 1981 has not been amended. In the first year the businessman will only get one half the capital cost allowance. Over the next three years they are going to lose $3 billion. It will come from the private sector to the public sector. I asked the Minister of Finance a question on June 30, 1982, after the measures which are formally being introduced into legislation this evening were announced. My question to the Minister of Finance was:
We on this side of the House welcome any measure that will assist small businesses in terms of development. But I point out to the Minister that on November 12 last year he brought in a provision with respect to capital cost allowance which has done more to prevent retooling and has dried up cash flow.
I asked the Minister of Finance whether or not he would adjust that. He said at that time:
If accepted, that would be a further large addition to the deficit which Hon. Members opposite have been complaining about-
I say to the Minister that if the private sector really is the engine of the economy, these traditional write-offs, these things which we have never ever thought of as loopholes, have to be given back.
Let us talk about the measure which the Minister has brought in. Where is the target? The Canadian Federation of Independent Business did a survey just recently and asked its more than 60,000 members this question. What do you anticipate doing with respect to your business? Are you going to lay people off as the result of the recession? Do you anticipate that you are going to stand pat and lay nobody off, or on the other hand are you going to expand? Seven per cent of the people who answered that survey said, "We are going to expand; we are going to create jobs; we are going to try". The target of this $400 million is the 7 per cent of the small business population which answered this survey in that way. The fact is that in this very deep recession, when people are squirreling their money away and are afraid to invest it, no one is expanding. There is no market demand; people are not making purchases.
When we ask when this $400 million offer will expire, the Minister tells us, in his comments, that it will expire by March 31 next year. The difficulty is that what that means is that we will be going through this recession until then, and when
November 8, 1982

recovery comes, as we hope it will, these moneys will not be available.
The people I am talking about in the small business community do not believe that the $400 million is going to be delivered for the purpose of expansion. I look forward to asking the Minister in Committee if everyone who meets the qualifications is going to be given the money. Will any discretion be exercised, or will anyone who meets the qualifications be given that money? I agree with the Minister that the small business community, which invests in the economy, should be given the money rather than it being given to consumers at a preferred rate. The 4 per cent rate is agreeable to me, but I want to make sure that the small business community gets the money.
There are a number of questions I should like to pose to the Minister with respect to this matter, but I gave him my word, Mr. Speaker, that we would not hold up the Bill. I shall comment again later in the proceedings, but I want this Bill to pass second reading this evening, so I restrict my comments to the foregoing.

Mr. Speaker, I have to assume that the Bill before us is the Government's response to the two years and $2 million spent on the small business financing review. From this long and expensive study, undertaken at a time when thousands small-businessmen have been going bankrupt, we get a three page Bill, at an estimated cost of $700,000 per page. The Minister proposes to spend less money to help small business than his Government gives almost every day of the week to large corporations in the country.
Small business is suffering a major illness akin to pneumonia, which today is treated with antibiotics. The Minister proposes to treat the major illness of small business with a mustard plaster, a kind of treatment which was used 50 years ago.
1 should like to look at what is happening to small business today. Since the fall of 1979, when interest rates began to rise, the increase in business bankruptcies has been phenomenal. They increased by 16.8 per cent in 1980, 22 per cent in 1981 and to date, in 1982, they have increased 40 per cent over last year. Businesses have been failing at the rate of about 200 each week. That is only the tip of the iceberg, Mr. Speaker. Some estimates show that as many as three to ten times as many businesses go into receivership, are liquidated by secured creditors or close their doors, as go into bankruptcy. The August figures for bankrupt businesses were 66 per cent higher than for August last year, with debtor liabilities reaching $133 million. The yearly total for debtor liabilities in 1982 is almost $1.5 billion, or more than all last year.
There are approximately 900,000 small business enterprises in Canada. This sector is vital to the Canadian economy because it employs four out of every ten Canadians and
Small Business Investment Grants Act
contributes 30 per cent of the total business gross national product. It is almost 100 per cent Canadian owned and pays a higher effective rate of tax than does large business; it pays a 33 per cent tax rate compared to 29 per cent for large business.
When the Government brought forward this Mickey Mouse proposal, this supposed solution to the problems of the small-businessman, it almost completely ignored the real facts of life. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business conducted a survey at the beginning of this year which showed that close to one-third of small businesses in the country would be forced to close down, sell part of their enterprise or be forced into bankruptcy if interest rates did not drop dramatically. At the time of that survey, interest rates had dropped about six points from the peak of August 1981. As the President of the CFIB, John Bulloch, pointed out, "It is precious little comfort to know that you are dying a little slower than you did last month". Yet this is how the Minister proposes to deal with this problem.
In the survey, the CFIB found, among other things, that 56 per cent of firms had cancelled expansion plans, due to high interest rates; 77 per cent saw profits shrink; over 10 per cent were already in the red, and 32 per cent had laid off workers in the last year. That was before the massive job losses we have seen this year.
Why is small business in such trouble? It is mainly due to two things, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it is because of the tremendous rate of unemployment; 12.7 per cent of the work force of this country, or almost 1,400,000 people, are unemployed. That is not counting the 250,000 to 400,000 people who have given up looking for work.
People who are unemployed have to cut back on the purchases they might have made if working. They do not take trips, which means the travel agent is in trouble; they cut back on buying clothes, which means the clothing store is in trouble; they buy cheaper grades of meat, which means the people in the food industry are in trouble, and I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker.
Many Canadians who have never been unemployed are cutting back because they do not know how long their present jobs will last. There is not a city in this country in which there are not some workers, ages 45 and under who have never been unemployed, but who are now unemployed, who see their friends and co-workers with less seniority than they, becoming unemployed. Even these people who are still working are holding on to their money because they are worried about what might happen to them next week or next month.
The 1,400,000 unemployed people drawing unemployment insurance benefits have enough to keep them alive, but substantially less than they were earning when they worked. Tens of thousands of the people drawing unemployment insurance benefits will be on welfare before they get back to work. It has been estimated that there are 800,000 people in this country receiving welfare, and that the number is increasing by about 10,000 each month. We are likely to have 14 per cent unemployment this winter, with the rate at which we are going and

November 8, 1982
Small Business Investment Grants Act
with the failure of the Government to do anything meaningful to deal with the problem. It is not surprising that small businesses are in trouble. Their former customers are simply not in the position to purchase goods and services as they did when they were working. That is the first reason small business is in trouble.
The second reason is the insane high interest rate policy which the Government has been following on the bad advice, as we on this side of the House have pointed out many times, of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. As a representative of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business pointed out to the House of Commons Finance Committee when it looked into the question of bank profits, nothing is more inhibiting to the health of small business or more destructive to the continued viability and existence of small business than the high interest rate policies with which we have lived for the last three or four years.
These policies are continuing. If we have interest rates at present which are lower than they were a few years ago, it is not because of conscious decisions by the Government or by the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Interest rates have come down because American interest rates have come down. They have come down there not because President Reagan realizes the importance of lower interest rates, but because the American economy is dead. No one wants to borrow money these days, even when interest rates are lower as they are in the United States.
This Bill proves what we already know, that Canadian small business is being strangled by the irresponsibility of the Government's high interest rate policies. As I have pointed out, the rate of bankruptcy has increased dramatically in the last couple of years. Bankruptcies are only a small illustration of what is happening in the country. Small business will not be bailed out by the federal Government, and this Bill demonstrates that small business is not very frequently aided at times of economic crisis, such as the current one.
The Government is cynical in offering this program in its present form to small business because it is limited in its reach and funding. At the same time as we debate this Bill, which will provide possibly $400 million to small business, the Government is imposing a $1.6 billion unemployment insurance premium increase on Canadians. This means that the very people who should be helping small business by increasing their purchases are having $1.6 billion taken out of their pockets.
The Bill will only aid small business after provincial programs with the same objectives have been utilized. Several Canadian provinces already have interest reduction grants; Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have such programs. The Federal Government's exposure is therefore not very great, with all its hyperbole about a major boost for small-businessmen.
Also a representative of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business stated to the review team, which as I pointed out earlier spent two years and $2 million looking into
the problems of small business, that "about 20 per cent of the small business community out there is solvent and capable of expanding." Where does that leave the other 80 per cent who are looking for working capital and refinancing? Obviously the chartered banks have neither the expertise to deal with small businesses financing problems nor the desire. A most important point raised by the small business review team concerned the discrimination small businesses experience when dealing with chartered banks and major financial institutions.
These banking institutions are tied to the major corporations. Major corporations have had no difficulty in obtaining assistance from the banks, yet small business has had real trouble in obtaining financial assistance, sound advice and understanding from them. Indeed, in recent months cases were brought to our attention by organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business where banks have been increasing the collateral required from small businesses for loans to 300, 400 or 500 per cent of the amount of the loan they were prepared to lend. We know the banks have been more than ready to lend hundreds of millions of dollars to the large corporations of the country. Much of that money was used in what turned out to be a very irresponsible manner. It was used to purchase and take over other companies, which added nothing to employment.
The Financial Times of October 18 reported that the amount of money owing to the big five banks in the country, most of which was borrowed for takeovers, amounted to $8.4 billion. This amount was in what were called non-productive loans, loans on which the companies were not meeting their payments on principal, the money which they borrowed, but in most cases, if not all, were not even meeting the interest payments. This is not the kind of treatment which banks are giving small business. Small businesses are being forced into bankruptcy, into receivership, to sell out or to close up.
We all know about the $1 billion loan payments which Dome Petroleum could not meet and the assistance which it received from the banks and the Government of Canada. Chrysler Canada received $200 million in federal loan guarantees from the Federal Government and $33 million from the Province of Ontario. Massey-Ferguson received $125 million in federal loan guarantees and $75 million from Ontario. These loans were made under the condition that these companies would continue to employ Canadian workers. These conditions have not been met; workers were laid off. Consolidated Computer Inc. received $125 million from the Federal Government before the Federal Government gave up and sold the firm; de Havilland Aircraft received $580 million; and Canadair received $1.3 billion. I could go on, but these are a few examples of the type of thing which has gone on continuously in the country recently. It is not surprising that these companies receive assistance and support from the Canadian Government and the banks, because the heads of the corporations which obtained the loans and the bail-outs were also directors of the banks, and the directors of the banks were also directors of the large corporations.

Let me read a few examples which I took from that book. Argus Corporation, which owned Massey-Ferguson at one time and Dominion Stores among others, had as its directors Conrad Black, who is director of Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, and Montague Black who is a director of the Toronto Dominion Bank. It is not surprising that Massey-Ferguson was able to obtain large loans from the banks.
The former head of CP Limited was Ian Sinclair, who is a director of the Royal Bank. The present President of CP is Fred Burbridge, who is a director of the Bank of Montreal.
The Hudson Bay Company, which is now owned by the Thompson interests, took over a number of companies and corporations, including FP Publications and Zellers. Kenneth Thompson is a director of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. George Richardson, who is the head of Hudson Bay, is a director of the Canadian Imperial Bank.
Walter Light is a director of Inco, a company which is in such great financial difficulty and which invested hundreds of millions of dollars in attempting to establish nickel mines which would compete, if successful, with Canadian mines where thousands of Canadians are now unemployed. It is a company which bought a battery firm and then wrote it off to the extent of $250 million. Walter Light is a director of the Royal Bank of Canada, and G. Arnold Hart is a director and executive officer of the Bank of Montreal.
Massey-Ferguson has one of its directors Alexander Runci-man, who is a director of the Royal Bank, and A. A. Thorn-brough, who is a director of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
I cited those examples for the record because they demonstrate very clearly what we have said so many times in this Party, that the large corporations in this country receive entirely different and much more sympathetic treatment than the small business people in this country.
The Minister tells us that under the provisions of this Bill the Government will be prepared to lend up to $400 million at financially attractive interest rates. First, it is unlikely that that money will be used because interest rates have come down since this Bill was prepared and many of those who would have qualified when the interest rates were higher will probably no longer qualify.
If one compares the $400 million to be made available to all of the small businesses in this country with the kind of treatment given to corporations such as Dome, Massey-Ferguson, Turbo and others, one can see where the interest, the support and the heart of this Liberal Government lies. It is not with the small business people who live and work in cities like Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. The Government's interests lie with the big business corporations which have always had the preference and attention which they believe they need.
As I indicated previously, this Bill will not come close to giving the small business community the help it needs. I would like to take a moment to explain our reason for this belief, aside from the fact that there is simply not enough money. If we understand this Bill correctly, it promises $400 million in
Small Business Investment Grants Act
assistance to small business. The program will provide an interest rate reduction of up to 4 per cent for loans between $10,000 and $500,000 taken out for the purchase of new capital equipment and buildings. The subsidy would be available for two years. Given the state of our economy and the fact that there are close to a million and a half unemployed, and given the fact that there are 400,000 less Canadians working in October of 1982 than were working in October of 1981, we must ask the Minister and the Government how many businessmen can or will invest in new capital equipment during these current economic conditions. For that reason we think that this Bill is insufficient. We believe that business must be aided in a serious manner, one which will give real thought to the problems of small business.
I would like to offer a few concrete proposals which we think should be undertaken. First, as we have said for a number of years now, a made-in-Canada interest rate policy must be established. We have been calling for an interest rate at one per cent above the rate of inflation. This change alone could assist many businesses now facing closure, to keep debt repayments current and stimulate consumer demand. Not only is small business suffering because of the high interest rates which we have had for the last couple of years, it has suffered inordinately because of the roller-coaster effect of those interest rates. No small-businessman can plan the operation of his business if he does not know whether the interest rates will be 14 per cent or 20 per cent, both of which he has seen in the last year.
We believe that the Bank Act must be revised. It should be changed to provide a proportion of bank lending to small business. This would prevent the situation which has plagued small businesses in the past number of years where, as I have already indicated, large corporate borrowers have tended to crowd out small businesses.
We believe that the Federal Business Development Bank needs to be restructured in order to provide real risk and venture capital to small firms and act as a clearing house for all Government programs for small business. The CASE program, counselling assistance for small enterprises, could also be strengthened and better integrated with the Federal Business Development Bank's granting of loans.
We need to provide assistance for small business in marketing. We believe that a more aggressive "buy Canadian" policy in both private and public sectors could assist small businesses to prosper. Promoting that message would be much more beneficial to Canadian business than the Government's current approach, which has been to sponsor an independent study with the banks showing that small-businessmen are not really being discriminated against by the banks, and then using the study in large scale advertisements in the major daily newspapers to tell small-businessmen that the banks are on their side.
You cannot kid the troops all the time, Mr. Speaker. The small-businessman who must deal with the banks' restrictive policies toward him knows that the bank is not his friend.

We believe that the Government should restore the small business bond. Small businesses in financial difficulty are the only ones eligible for these bonds now. These bonds will terminate on December 31 of this year. Small-businessmen need access to lower rate funds for both new investment and to finance inventory costs. We would continue to offer this vehicle to small-businessmen for development purposes and operating loans.
We do not intend to hold this Bill up. As I indicated earlier, we believe that it is a very small step toward helping the small business community in this country.
Having said that it is a very small step, we do not intend to prolong the debate unnecessarily. I want to say to the Minister that small business will not be very thankful to the Government when it sees the results of this Bill. They will not get much help from the Bill, not the kind of help they need and deserve if this country is to prosper.

Mr. Speaker, for many reasons I am very pleased to have an opportunity to make a brief intervention on the Bill, particularly when the small business investment grant seems to be condemned before it has even had a chance to go anywhere. That is what I seem to be hearing in the House, although I must confess that the business community of northwestern Ontario, with which I have many dealings now, as I have had in the past, seems to look with favour on this particular Bill and anxiously awaits its passage.
I suppose the problem with an item which only amounts to $400 million is that the critics of the Government will immediately say that it is not enough to put one and a half million people suddenly back to work. I think that the Minister tried to make it very clear in his opening remarks that the intent of the Bill was not to put everyone back to work all at once because, Lord knows, we all wish we had that magic button, some miraculous item which would do all those things instantaneously. But the message, both in and out of the Government, is that it will take many things working in harmony to make things happen, to get people back to work, to restore confidence, and so on.
I believe that we are now beginning to see many signs across the country and around the world that we will stay within Canada, because Hon. Members opposite say, "Quit blaming it on the rest of the world". We somehow live in the little world of our own, and the rest of it does not count, so we will stay within our boundaries for the purpose of the exercise.
I would say that I am happy with the Bill because it is another sign which states that small business generates jobs and activity within Canada and makes work within Canada available to other Canadians. That is a very commendable idea. While Hon. Members opposite want to put down the small amount invested in this particular program, I know they are as anxious, as we are, to see it implemented as quickly as possible, to give small business, which has the ability to expand
through research, development and generally to allow their business to grow, to do just that with some modicum of help.
Basically, the business community operates best on its own and sometimes only needs a little bit of encouragement to get going. The small business investment grant will give many an opportunity, through spending some money on research and providing money for new capital equipment, to begin to expand. That begs the question: are there businesses around which have the ability to invest and to expand? Daily we listen to a litany of statistics which spell out doom and gloom.
