The statistics and the reality are there, except that they stand alone. I think that if one has a problem or a series of problems, one must try to identify them. The trouble with these statistics, as true as they are, is that they leave the impression that all is wrong everywhere. We know that we have many sad problems in Sudbury. We know why. We know we have many sad problems in the automotive industry. Those of us who drive Canadian-made vehicles say, "Well, at least I did not contribute to that problem". Maybe those of us who have elected, for whatever good reason, to buy foreign-made vehicles might want to consider our action. However, the free enterprise system is such that we buy what we want, and so on.
I find that in the doom and gloom which is being spread, we are not getting a handle on matters as they are, because there are contradictions out there. Excuse me for going beyond our borders, but right now, primarily because of the American market situation, pulp and paper products and lumber products from northwestern Ontario are basically sold south of the border. Therefore, we have a decline. Yet for some strange reason, a gentleman who sells power chain saws only to the commercial sector, to the professional cutter, tells me that he is having the best year ever. I asked him, "Well, why is that?" He said, "It is because they are really thinking of the future. They are working hard, and I must tell you something. I am working harder than 1 have worked in the last 25 years, but I find that when I work harder the results are there". I also find that in my community, even with the doom and gloom, many businessmen are saying, "1 am looking forward to the passage of Bill C-136 because my small business is capable of investment."
I know a jeweller. One does not have to buy watches, rings and china to know a jeweller. He said to me, "Mr. Masters, I have had to hire more staff." I asked, "How could you do that in these difficult times when there is no money around? How can you expand your business?" He said, "It is because I was running scared. I stayed home and I worked. I sat down with my staff and asked them how we could meet competition and make sure that we did well". That man is doing well. I know people in other sectors of the economy who are in fact expanding now. They are hardy souls, and I think most businessmen in Canada are hardy souls, and they are working at it.
Therefore, I say that the small business investment grant will help not only those in northwestern Ontario but all those across Canada who look for a silver lining as well, those who
November 8, 1982

look forward to making their businesses better and more competitive and are anxious to take advantage of the help which is inherent in this sum of S400 million which will be put at their disposal. They are anxious to put it to work. I say, "Thank goodness for the small-businessman because he is our hope now and in the future". The amount small-businessmen spend of this money in order to add some modest extension to their businesses or to do some meaningful research to help them grow will have a tremendous spin-off effect. This is because one small-businessman who does something leads to another small-businessman having to do something else. It is just another small cog in the wheel which is starting to turn toward progress, but we will not make progress if we steadfastly cling to the idea that there is no hope. What I think, conclusively, is that there is hope. Bill C-136 offers more hope at least to one small segment of the business community which will take advantage of it. This, combined with many other initiatives is in fact what will turn things on more and more.
However, there is one other aspect upon which I would like to comment briefly before I sit down. This particular Bill is part of the ongoing consultative process between business and Government.

Members in the House and to people across the country what is the difficulty with the consultative practice, because I sat down some time ago with eight businessmen. So I listened to them and they suddenly began, in this consultative process, to say to me, "We now see the difficulty. I think that is a message for the whole country, and the message is simple. We must begin to accentuate the positive. We must remember that the country will make progress if we work together, if we think together, if we become more conscious of one another as Canadians. I think the Government has the message well in mind when it introduces legislation such as the small business investment grant, which will indeed help small businesses across the country carry out meaningful research and expand. To me, it is another item of encouragement to the country. I think I will now sit down because I know all Hon. Members want to see the Bill put through the committee stage as quickly as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope to abbreviate my remarks. I am very pleased to have the opportunity of explaining this legislation to the House. The proposed legislation makes some modifications to the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan which was first introduced in the budget of November 12, 1981. It might be useful if I took a few moments to explain the details.
Hon. Members will remember that when it was first introduced, it offered assistance to home owners who are having difficulty renewing their mortgages at high rates of interest. The assistance was available to those people whose mortgage payments on renewal would amount to more than 30 per cent of their income. That is very much the principle involved here. It is of assistance to those having to pay more than 30 per cent of their income. At that time it was felt that for people who had substantial equity in their home, the original plan would offer a guarantee of up to $3,000 if the lenders would agree to defer interest payments. In the case of people who had no substantial equity and were paying out more than 30 per cent of their income in mortgage payments, there was an outright grant of up to $3,000.
In the intervening months if became evident that in the uncertain economic climate of the time, many Canadians felt that deferring interest payments on their mortgage was perhaps not the best solution to their personal financial problems. The demand for interest deferral guarantees was not as great as expected, even taking into account that interest rates had already begun to decline.
This feeling was particularly strong in parts of the country where house prices have begun to drop and the home owners' equity was being reduced.

November 8, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
Responding to the changing circumstances, the former minister of Finance, in his budget statement of June 29, announced that the interest deferral aspect of the plan would be eliminated. In future, all those borrowers who qualified for assistance under the plan would receive an outright grant, regardless of how much equity they might have in their home. All those who until that time had qualified for an interest deferral guarantee would receive the grant instead. The Bill now before us gives effect to the changes that I have described.
The principle of this legislation has been debated at some length and approved by the House on previous occasions, that is, the idea of providing assistance to people who may be in danger of losing their homes, giving them some breathing space in which they can make some adjustment in their financial arrangements. There are no new principles involved in this Bill. The intention is the same, and I hope that members on all sides of the House will agree to deal with it expeditiously.
There is, in fact, some urgency to put this legislation into effect. Since June 29, CMHC has approved $3,000 grants for more than 6,000 families, but cheques cannot be sent to them until this amendment to the National Housing Act has been approved by Parliament and proclaimed. This number includes not only people who have applied for assistance since June 29, but some 2,000 persons who were qualified before that date for interest-deferral guarantees and are now to receive the grants instead.
I would like, at this stage, to express a word of appreciation to the financial institutions which are very much involved in the administration of this plan. Borrowers who wish to take part in it are asked to approach their mortgage lenders who will discuss their particular problem in detail and assist them in completing the application forms and forwarding them to CMHC. I am assured by my predecessor and the officials at CMHC that the lending institutions, banks, trust companies, credit unions, caisses populates, and the like, have been most co-operative and have generally been very anxious to help borrowers to arrive at a solution which would help them to keep their homes.
I think we can all take some satisfaction that the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan has not been used as much as we had anticipated nearly a year ago when interest rates, as Hon. Members well know, were at an historic peak. The fact remains, however, that the plan, in its proposed improved form, is still there for people who are truly in need.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has indicated, a realistic projection of the economy for the year ahead indicates that although the inflation rate will drop, the number of those in the work force who will be without jobs will remain high. These circumstances will inevitably create problems for some families in managing their mortgage payments. I hope that, in these circumstances, borrowers will discuss their situation with their mortgage lenders to discover whether the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan can be useful to them through the hard times or whether some other arrangements can be arrived at which will help them to keep their homes.
If I emphasize home ownership in these remarks, it is because that is the subject of the Bill before us, assistance for mortgage renewal. At the same time, I would like to make it clear that the Government's concern is for the housing of all Canadians, whether they occupy it as home owners, as tenants, or by some other form of tenure.
With these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Members opposite for their courtesy, and again apologize for my tardy arrival, which I hope will be corrected because the telephone assistants are hard at work at the moment.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my old friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) who is responsible for Housing on his first Bill in this House. 1 know he will bring to this portfolio the same degree of dedication which he had in his previous portfolio. Having said that, I know the Minister does not expect to get off without having addressed the real problems facing the housing industry in this country, namely, that of availability, affordability and the acute decline in housing starts. We supported this Bill, the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, when it was first introduced to the House, and at the time we raised very serious reservations about the limitations which where placed on it at that time. The Government has now come to recognize the validity of these criticisms and is in fact extending the application of the Bill. That is the least they could do, given the circumstances under which this Bill is introduced. I am sorry the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) is not in the House because he is largely responsible for the mess that the Minister of Public Works responsible for Housing has inherited. I would have liked to have heard the Minister make some reference to the recommendations of the Lortie Committee, the famous blue ribbon committee which was supposed to address the keystone of the Government's housing policy, namely, the provision whereby they would reduce mortgage interest rates anywhere from 4 per cent to 6 per cent.
That provision, as Hon. Members know, was turned down by the Lortie Commission. They recommended against it because of the distortions it would have on the marketplace. But it is well to put on the record what the former minister responsible for housing said with respect to that measure when he spoke on "The Nation's Business" on Sunday, July 11, 1982. With respect to the deliberations of the Lortie Committee, he said, "the Canadian Government will implement a system for providing loans at 3 to 6 per cent below the market rate to ensure your long-term security". There were no ifs, and's or but's, no qualifications. There was a firm, unequivocal commitment to proceed with the implementation of that measure. Indeed, when the former minister of finance brought down his June budget and introduced this measure, he said at the time, and I believe I am paraphrasing him correctly, when he referred the measure to this committee, that he could not conceive of a situation whereby the committee would recommend against the implementation of that measure. In addition,
November 8, 1982

the former minister said in an interview in The Toronto Star, again in July: "There's no question of chance. The plan will be implemented. The Government is committed to it."
We know of course now from the new Minister of Finance that they are not going to proceed. They are going to recommend that the recommendations of the Lortie Commission be accepted because of the disruptions the plan would have on the market place. And I say, rightly so, because, again, we cautioned the Government on the way they were proceeding in terms of restricting the application of the mortgage reduction scheme to new houses.
The reason I raise that at this particular time is because what the Government proposes today will not go very far in addressing the problem. Indeed, to use an old Parliamentary cliche, I would not even describe it as band-aid treatment. What is the situation the Minister has inherited? The bad news for August: housing starts during August were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 87,000 for all areas, when we should have for the year somewhere in the vicinity of 220,000. I refer the Minister to the actual housing starts for the end of the third quarter for all areas of Canada which stood at 88,950. At that rate we will be lucky if we get to 130,000 at the end of the year when we actually need, according to the figures provided to us by CMHC, somewhere in the vicinity of 220,000 starts just to keep abreast of demand.
What does the Government propose to do instead of the mortgage reduction scheme which was turned down by the Lortie Commission to provide some degree of security to those potential home buyers who are looking at the marketplace, looking at the fluctuations in interest rates? Take a look at what has happened over the past year. Canadians are in no way encouraged to enter into a mortgage agreement, because God only knows what is going to happen in the months ahead. There is no security against cyclical fluctuations in interest rates such as have plagued the industry for the past year. That is what the Government intended to address in that measure. It is interesting that the Minister said, in order to provide for your long-term security the Government will implement a scheme to reduce mortgage interest payments. I say to the Government it should have made that program universal in its application. If it had done so by way of a tax credit or tax deduction, it would have provided the real and immediate stimulation to the housing industry to get housing starts up to where they should be. That move, Sir, would be a matter of enlightened self-interest because when we talk about the unemployment situation in the country today, we should do so in the context of the housing crisis.
We have unemployment somewhere between 12 per cent and 13 per cent. Over 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed. Yet both the Minister and the Government know that one way of addressing the unemployment problem in a very meaningful way is to address the housing crisis. Housing is a very labourintensive industry, an industry capable of providing 2.5 jobs for every housing unit started in the country, and capable of producing anywhere from $6,000 to $10,000 per unit in
National Housing Act (No. 2)
Government revenues. Why the Government has not proceeded to make this plan universal in its application just boggles the mind. I do not believe the Government can hide behind the excuse that interest rates are down right now. No one, certainly not the Government, can assure us of just how long that situation will last.
When we speak of the housing crisis, Mr. Speaker, we are talking in terms of not only housing starts and availability, but affordability. One of the concerns I have, and this certainly will be brought to the Government's attention in the committee stage of this Bill, is that of the Canada Rental Supply Plan. That plan was to produce 30,000 rental units by providing long-term interest free loans. We know, Sir, that up to October 26 there had been only 7,814 applications. I repeat, applications, and it is important to make that distinction because if this represented 7,814 starts, that would be significant. But these are merely applications. We do not know how many actual starts there are. I suspect the number is probably significantly lower than the 7,814 applications out of 30,000. That means, of course, that builders are just not taking advantage of this program. The reason for that, Sir, is the market place, rent controls, because of the wide disparity between market rent and economic rent. Given costs today, given the return a developer can realize on rental units, it is just not economically feasible for him to proceed, interest-free loans notwithstanding.
I suggest to the Minister seriously that he should give consideration to scrapping the Canada Rental Supply Plan and putting that money into co-op housing as there is a real need for low-income housing right across the country. That money would be taken up very quickly and it would provide a quick stimulation to the industry and badly needed low-cost housing to Canadians right across the country. Why the Government has not moved in this direction, Mr. Speaker, is very difficult to understand. I hope the Minister, when he speaks to the Bill in committee, will address himself to that problem. Certainly we are in a serious situation.
In addition to the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, all the Government offers is the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan and the Canada Home Renovation Plan. That, Sir, is not going to come close to addressing the problems we are facing in the nation today. Indeed, let us take a look at the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan whereby the Government provides $3,000 grants to first-time home buyers. As of October 22, 1982, CMHC had approved 63,862 applications. This figure includes 22,495 applications for new housing and 41,367 applications for existing homes. In other words, less than half the grants were used for new housing. In other words, the program designed to stimulate new housing is not in fact having that effect. As far as the Canada Home Renovation Plan is concerned, the $3,000 grants under this program were to be directed to those individuals who wanted to convert some portion of their home into an apartment unit for a relative or an in-law or what have you, and that would go a long way to filling a need. In other words, it would provide

November 8, 1982
National Housing Act (No. 2)
affordable housing for young people just starting out or for elderly people, or what have you. However, it still remains restricted and the shortcomings of the program are not addressed by this Bill. Consequently, we will not have an opportunity to move on it by way of amendment. But certainly we will have a chance to ask the Minister to address these problems when it gets into committee.
I want to assure the Minister it is our intention to co-operate with him to get this Bill out of the House and out of committee as expeditiously as possible. I say that with some reservations because we do want to take the opportunity to hear from the Minister and CMHC officials and, hopefully, from people in the industry as to just exactly how they view the situation out there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to address a few remarks to Bill C-135, the amendments to the National Housing Act. This Bill is intended to implement the June budget changes to the housing measures originally announced in the November budget. The Bill does a couple of things. First, it changes the term of the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan so that homeowners with monthly mortgages and property tax payments in excess of 30 per cent of the gross family income will qualify for a $3,000 grant rather than interest deferral. Formerly, only homeowners with less than 5 per cent equity in their homes and with payments in excess of 30 per cent could qualify for these grants. Other homeowners would have had only the option of deferring interest, which would have been added on to their principal and the deferral would have to have been guaranteed by CMHC. Since it was almost impossible to qualify for the grant, the Government did in fact change the terms of the plan to allow some homeowners to in fact qualify for this program.
Secondly, the amendments to the National Housing Act will provide an extension to this plan for a second year. Originally, the plan was to terminate on November 12, 1982 but the June budget has extended it to December 31, 1983. In terms of the National Housing Act, I would acknowledge that these changes are an improvement, but still, they do not address the real problems of housing in Canada today. There are no changes in areas where they are so necessary such as rental housing, co-operative housing and low-cost housing which is so necessary at the present time.
In the City of Winnipeg there is a problem which I am sure exists in many other areas of the country as well. Through a program called Limited Dividend Housing, private investors have received large government subsidies to enable them to build lucrative rental units. One of the conditions of the subsidy was that any application for rental increases would have to be approved by CMHC. It bothers me that in the City of Winnipeg, as was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), and I am sure this has happened in other areas of the country as well, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has allowed rental increases well beyond the six and five that we are supposed to
be adhering to at the present time. I am bothered that the Government can make the plan apply to some people, but that others who do not wish to comply with its conditions do not have to do so. That is unfair and unjust. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James says that we should make them roll back the rent increases to comply with the six and five program, and I think he is right.
The rental housing that was supposed to have been supplied under the Canada Rental Supply Unit Plan provided in Bill C-89, and was supposed to come into effect earlier this year, promised 30,000 rental starts. In fact, by October this year less than 25 per cent of that number had been committed by CMHC. Out of the 30,000 rental units allocated in March 1982, only 7,341 had been approved by CMHC as of October 4. I am concerned about this because of the high cost of rental accommodation in the country and the low vacancy rates in many areas.
The Government's approach with Bill C-135, is symptomatic of its tendancy to apply band-aids when new systems are needed. I hope that the Minister responsible for CMHC will read the comments I make tonight and, as a result, will ask officials in his Department to look into the feasibility of the proposal I am about to make.
Canadians find themselves in an increasingly difficult position if they want to own their own home, Mr. Speaker. I see nothing wrong with people renting a home, living in co-op housing or low-cost housing all their lives. An expectation has been built up in our society, however, that people may own their home, but that ideal is rapidly becoming out of reach for most people. When my grandparents lived on the farm they built their house for very little. When I bought my house in The Battlefords, it cost a great deal. In fact, many people of my age will have to spend one-third of the income they would expect to earn in a lifetime, to provide shelter for their families. If things continue in this way, then in my children's time or in my grandchildren's time, housing may not be affordable at all.
Instead of applying different methods to the same system, I think we should consider different systems by which people could own their homes. I should like the Minister in charge of CMHC to ask his bureaucrats to consider developing a program through the high schools which would teach young people how to build their own homes. I have mentioned this before and some people think the suggestion of a course in building as a mandatory part of education, is rather farfetched. But unless something like this happens, Mr. Speaker, in years to come only the elite in our society will be able to afford to own a home.
If such a program were developed by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Provinces were encouraged to include it in their educational system, it would go a long way toward helping people to provide shelter for themselves. If we had a course called "How to Build a House"-and that is a simplistic way of putting it, I suppose-as part of our educational system, then when people graduated from school or
November 8, 1982

university and entered the working world where they would have to shift for themselves without much help from the Government or from their families, they would have three options. First, those people who could not afford to buy housing would at least be able to put their "sweat equity" into it. All they would require would be the materials which they would acquire by the means available to them. Second, those people who quite often are taken advantage of by housing programs or fly-by-night contractors, could supervise the quality control of their homes as they are being built. Possibly, in their free time they could also put in some "sweat equity" toward the downpayment for the house. Third, another group of people who could afford to buy under the present system, could have the housing contractor build the house for them.
In the future, I think such a system could give us the best of all worlds or at least a better housing system than we have at present. The day is rapidly coming when the present system will not work, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canadians are afraid, small business is afraid, the banks are afraid. The banks are tightening up credit markets, calling in loans-

The Tories are afraid.
November 8, 1982

You are right, the Tories are afraid. The NDP is afraid. Canadians generally are afraid. They are afraid because business and jobs are falling and being lost around them again and again. As these credit markets tighten up, more real jobs are being lost and jobs that could have been created are not being created.
Banks are tight for money because, in conjunction with the federal Government, they are bailing out huge corporations that have proven themselves unsuccessful. How can we condone again and again and again corporations borrowing from the banks to bail themselves out, the Government guaranteeing those bailouts and further subsidizing them with extensive taxpayers' money?
One billion dollars for Dome Petroleum, $34 million for Maislin, millions more for Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson and Canadair tightens the money markets for small companies, making it impossible for them to borrow in order to sustain themselves in a cash flow crisis which at any other time would in fact not occur.
The reality is that as the consumptive market declines, as it has declined, consumption drops and cash flow falls with it. In spite of heavy inventories that many companies have, long records of successful borrowing and repayment, without that consumptive demand, as the cash flow falls and high inventories, we see a series of bankruptcies, and the number in fact increases. The Government attempts that solution again and again. The Government borrows more money; the Government taxes more. It takes more and more of the credit that should be available to small businesses. In effect, they have borrowed $21.2 billion so far this year. With a $23 billion deficit, they stand before us and threaten to borrow more.
The perverse practice of encouraging mismanagement and failure to the detriment of a healthy atmosphere for successful enterprise has caused severe damage to our industrial structure and economic fabric. We have become a guaranteed society rather than the just society promised by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Government will guarantee everything for unprofitable ventures.
If you are big enough.

That's right, if you are big enough-the big ones, the big guys. The little guys; forget it!
This type of corporate cradle to the grave-the NDP understand about cradle to the grave-dependency breeds its own insecurity. Corporations are not living by the capitalist Darwinism of competition because they know that they will not be rewarded, but that they will be rewarded for incompetence by a Federal Government bailout.
How many jobs will be lost? How many jobs will not be created because of this Government's policy? We are facing the worst unemployment since 1936. Unemployment is rising, and even more jobs are disappearing. Last year, 1,900 jobs a day disappeared, largely because of the record number of small businesses that went into bankruptcy. Unemployment is running at 12.7 per cent nationally and 14.2 per cent in British Columbia. Small business would help to alleviate these grim
Adjournment Debate
statistics by creating new and permanent jobs. In the United States in the past six months the number of people with jobs has grown by 209,000. In Canada, the number of people with jobs in the same period dropped by 269,000. While the U.S. is growing, we are losing, and they were ahead in the race, to begin with.
If small businesses are not allowed access to credit, to expand, prosper and create jobs, how will Canadians find fulfilment in the work ethic that is inherent and vital to our culture? What is the Government doing to create real jobs? There is a great difference between real jobs and community development programs which create temporary jobs which may last 20 weeks or some small part of a year and then disappear.
As for the $1 million that is provided to my constituency in these programs, which may create from 60 to 80 jobs, I wonder what would happen if we divided that evenly, even in $10,000, $50,000 or $100,000 grants to a few individual, permanent businesses in our riding, businesses which would create real jobs. I have many examples of these businesses in my own riding.
One particular constituent had a proposal to computerize automobile repair facilities. That sounds like a good idea. He intended to capitalize on the high tech revolution. He proposed to create five real jobs. That may not be very many, but the needed capital was not forthcoming from the FDB, in spite of the inventory, and assets of this gentleman. The Bank asked about the cash flow. This in fact, would indicate that a guarantee is needed, with support for that small business.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member is using Standing Order 40 to express his concerns this evening. I have read the Hon. Member's question of October 29 and I listened to his remarks tonight.
The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) states a concern for jobs lost as a result of his assumption of reduced credit availability, but he completely ignores the negative employment consequences which would have arisen had the companies he mentioned, Dome, Maislin, Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson, and so on, not received financial support. Had there been no support for these companies, the Hon. Member would have been the first one to stand in his place tonight and complain that the Government was responsible for the resulting job losses.
Secondly, the Hon. Member makes no mention of the interest rate relief programs which were introduced over the last year to ease the burden for farmers, small-businessmen, first time home buyers and mortgage renewers. These programs have gone a good distance toward easing the pressures on these borrowers during very difficult times.

November 8, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Most importantly, however, the Hon. Member appears to have a confused notion of the mechanics of credit availability. He argues that the directing of funds toward support of certain companies will reduce the credit available to other borrowers and put upward pressure on interest rates. What he has failed to mention, Mr. Speaker, is that during part of the period that this financial assistance occurred, the bank rate dropped some 500 basis points from its peak in June. Mortgage rates are also down 500 basis points and other interest rates are following suit. This decline in interest rates is obviously making it easier, not harder, to borrow.
Why has this happened? Obviously, interest rate developments in the United States have had an important impact on domestic interest rates. As well, an important determinant of interest rates, and therefore of credit availability, is the overall balance between the demand for and supply of funds in Canada. During the recession, private-sector borrowing in Canada weakened substantially and the personal-sector savings rose to historically high levels. The supply of loanable funds increased markedly relative to the demand, and this has helped put downward pressure on interest rates. Under these circumstances, the directing of financial support to the private sector, in amounts which are very small relative to the total supply of credit, has not influenced interest rates and has therefore no significant influence on the total amount of credit available to other borrowers, as the Hon. Member would like to lead Canadians to believe.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I find it very disturbing that the Hon. Member would try to instill this kind of fear and no confidence in our country rather than trying to build trust, cooperation and work together to build confidence in this country so that we can have a recovery.

Mr. Speaker, on June 29, this year, a minor official of Public Works in St. John's, Newfoundland, was sentenced to prison for one year for having taken a $800 kick-back. Clearly, Sir, our system of justice was quite efficient in this particular case. By coincidence, the next day, June 30, I raised questions in the House, with the then Minister of Public Works, concerning the multimillion dollar debacle at the Montreal postal facilities. The Minister promised an answer, while the Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation said he had no indication that there was anything wrong. I later received a letter from the then Minister of Public Works who said, "problems have indeed occurred and have either been fully resolved or are in the process of resolution". That was a curious admission by the Minister.
On July 6 1 asked more questions of the then Minister of Public Works. He changed his tune slightly and said he was looking into the matter, but he hoped that if the facts I brought out were incorrect I would apologize. Getting nowhere
with the Minister, I wrote to the Auditor General on September 30, 1982 asking him to institute an audit of the construction of the Montreal postal facilities. On October 1 the Auditor General replied saying that he shared my concern about cost overruns on major projects. He also felt there was sufficient information on the problems associated with the project to enable appropriate action to be taken by those involved and those concerned. He recommended that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts of the House of Commons should proceed with an investigation.
Two days later, Mr. Speaker, I issued a press release again urging the Government to level with the public; if not, Members of Parliament should put additional information on the record. In the interim, Canada's daily newspapers had launched their own investigation and came to their own conclusions, calling the Montreal affair a "horror story" and claiming that millions were squandered. It appears that after four years of apparently intensive investigation by the Commercial Crime Branch of the RCMP, charges were laid against only three individuals who seem to be bit players. My concern, Sir, is with the main actors. Here are some major players and some questions to be answered.
How did a corporation named ABBDL and T. Pringle and Sons succeed, against the advice of the staff of Public Works, in securing a substantial contract-millions of dollars, Sir-as design consultants for the three postal terminal projects in Montreal? How were these design consultants able to claim up to 82 hours a week of work per employee performed on the project? How were the same design consultants able to claim $250,000 per month, each month, for the duration of the contract, over and above payroll costs?
How did a corporation named Techmont obtain a sizeable contract for soil studies at the sites, as it appears that this rather strange corporation had been created by the original directors of the design consultants who, of course, were ABBDL and so on?
Who bears the specific responsibility for making it possible to award work to a company named Claude Theberge and Associates who, on direct ministerial order, received a sizeable contract for interior design?
Who are the principles in the corporation named Signalis Inc., a corporation which was awarded a signage contract at the facility, in view of the fact that this corporation was a fully owned subsidiary of Claude Theberge and Associates and was created only three months before the contract was awarded?
I am not speaking about an $800 bribe, or a few thousand dollars, I am speaking of $50 million given-or paid-in the final analysis to these consultants-that is over $8 million more than the originally estimated total cost of the whole project.
Can the Department justify payments to Miron Construction of $162,000, Beaver Asphalt of $34,000 and Cegeco Construction of $343,000 for extra work done allegedly
November 8, 1982

because of lack of knowledge of soil conditions when several contracts had been previously awarded to other companies to study these very soil conditions on the sites?
Who are the principals behind Shawinigan Engineering and La Societe Dyname who were awarded, against the advice of the staff of Public Works, a sizeable contract, as project managers? There is also the question of the landscaping consultants, Schrieber-Williams with sizeable cost over-runs.
All of these are referred to, of course, in the report which was made available to The Globe and Mail in the spirit of the freedom of information legislation. That, at least, is a hopeful sign. The Public Works (Canada) follow-up audit of the map project in Montreal is where all these matters and others can be found.
1 could go on, Mr. Speaker, but my time is passing so I shall close by asking what the political and legal responsibilities are of the consecutive Ministers of Public Works under whose direction and guidance these shenanigans took place. I refer to colleagues and former colleagues such as the Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube, Hon. C. M. (Bud) Drury, Hon. Judd Buchanan and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet).
Where is the element of accountability, where tens of millions of dollars are lost in the same way as over $100 million was lost in the Consolidated Computer debacle? Where is the element of accountability?
To paraphrase the infamous Dr. Joseph Goebbels, if you want to get away with a lie, it had better be a big lie. In the same way, if you want to get away with mismanagement and patronage, it had better be on a large scale. That appears to be exactly what happened here, to the detriment of the taxpayers of Canada.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-CONSTRUCTION OF MONTREAL POSTAL TERMINAL. (B) QUERY RESPECTING DIFFICULTIES DURING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to provide a more detailed answer to the question raised in the House of Commons by the member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) on June 30, regarding a large postal establishment in Montreal. Before going any further, I may add that the Hon. Member received a reply from the Minister of Public Works at the time (Mr. Cosgrove), which reads as follows, and 1 shall quote the letter in English. I hope my hon. colleague will bear with my English which is less than fluent.

Dear Mr. MacKay:
Re: Metropolitan Area Postal Plant Montreal. P.Q.
I refer to your question in the House on June 30, 1982 concerning possible problems with the construction of the Metropolitan Area Postal Plant in Montreal, Quebec.
As you know, in the construction of any project of this magnitude it is inevitable that problems could occur in any of the multitude of activities inherent to such a complex project during its implementation. With regard to this specific project, problems have indeed occurred and have either been fully resolved or are in the process of resolution.
Adjournment Debate
While it would be very time consuming and costly to gather the complex details of every problem, I would be happy to oblige you if you could be more precise as to the particular problem area of your concern.
Thank you very much for your interest.
Yours truly,
Paul Cosgrove.

Mr. Speaker, in 1974 Treasury Board approved the appropriation of $161 million in 1974 dollars for the construction of postal establishments in the Montreal area. The entire project included a new mail-sorting centre in downtown Montreal, an annex to the Laval postal station and a new bulk-mail routing centre and mail-sorting centre in Ville St. Laurent. The Treasury Board authorization allowed for the inflation factor and called for an overall cost of $212 million, a figure that was to be used as the basis for all subsequent estimates connected with the project. As the project materialized, it was found on the basis of certain data that it would have to be expanded, which resulted in a certain amount of delay. As a result, a new authorization was obtained from the Treasury Board in 1977, establishing a new budget for $241.6 million, and this plus indexation raised the total estimated cost to $254.3 million.

CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-TRANSFER OF REPAIR WORK FROM WINNIPEG TO MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 24 Wilson Parasiuk, the MLA for Transcona and I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to express our concern about CN's announcement the previous week that it was considering the consolidation of its passenger repair work at the Point St. Charles shops in Montreal at the expense of the Transcona shops in Winnipeg. We reacted strongly to this possibility because we had reason to believe that CN was not really considering the matter with an open mind, but had really already made up its mind and was just going through the motions.
On September 29 Mr. LeClair, the President of CNR, wrote a letter to the Minister of Transport, and shortly thereafter Mr. LeClair acknowledged our letter of September 24, saying that he had written to the Minister of Transport and that we would likely be hearing from him shortly with a more detailed response to our concern.
As of today, November 8, over six weeks later, we have yet to hear from the Minister of Transport directly. When I asked him about this on November 1, he seemed to indicate that he had no intention of ever answering our letter. Instead the Minister of Transport referred to a letter from Mr. LeClair which he said he sent out to all concerned about the issue, a statement which is completely untrue. He has never sent me

November 8, 1982
Adjournment Debate
anything on this issue at all. I can only assume that the letter from Mr. LeClair to the Minister of Transport, which the Minister falsely claimed he sent out, is Mr. LeClair's letter of September 29 that I did not receive from the Minister, but a copy of which I had the opportunity to study.
The letter tried to cover up what CN was really doing. It tried to explain the reduction of coach work in Transcona because of a general reduction in coach work across the system as a result of the VIA cutbacks. The truth is otherwise. What is happening and what is at issue is that the share of the passenger work which Transcona traditionally received is projected to be drastically altered in 1983 from 40 per cent to 5 per cent which as I see it is a transfer, not just an adjustment. Mr. LeClair and the Minister of Transport have never denied these figures. Instead they have hidden behind generalities about continued high levels of employment at Transcona and vague promises of expanded freight work.
In Mr. LeClair's letter of September 29 he talked about the expansion of the wheel shop and the program to build 300 woodchip cars at Transcona. What he did not say was that both these programs were near completion and that therefore neither of them would in any way compensate for the loss of coach work in 1983 or in subsequent years. Some 230 jobs will be directly affected and another 70 or so indirectly, for a total of 300 jobs. At least a hundred of these jobs-those of the sheetmetal workers, pipefitters, electricians and machinists- could not be replaced by expanded freight work. Even carmen would be affected because, contrary to the ignorant remark of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) several weeks ago on this issue that there was no difference between upholstering a cushion and working on a boxcar, coach work is a source of preferred work for senior tradesmen. The Minister of Employment was invited to work under a boxcar for a while to clear his mind. In all likelihood he has never been inside a railway shop, never mind a boxcar.
There is a cover up going on. The Minister of Transport and the Minister of Employment are in cahoots with the new President of CNR who is determined to do to the rest of the railway what his predecessor did to CN Express and CN passenger service; that is destroy it, by forgetting that the railway is not like any other business and cannot be run just according to short-term profit margins. This is all the more reprehensible when it is being done by a Crown corporation.
What is even more reprehensible is the way the Minister of Employment is acting. He has deserted Winnipeg and is acting like a hypocrite, celebrating the new Air Canada facilities in Winnipeg while helping cover up this significant transfer of work out of Winnipeg; either that or he is a pathetic, ill-informed stooge of the CNR. In any case, it is about time he smartened up and got on side before we have a repeat of the
Air Canada overhaul work transfer from Winnipeg to Montreal, a transfer for which this time he will shoulder most of the blame.
Does the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) have anything to say in defence of his Minister? Does he have anything to say on this issue at all? We have not received any answers from anybody on this, and I am looking forward to seeing whether he will actually tell us something, or whether he will have a well-rehearsed statement designed to tell us absolutely nothing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-TRANSFER OF REPAIR WORK FROM WINNIPEG TO MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in all fairness to the Chamber I should refuse to reply to the Hon. Member opposite. Any Member who stands and calls a Minister of this House a hypocrite and a stooge should be asked to withdraw those statements. I should refuse to answer the Hon. Member unless he learns some decorum in the House. However, for the sake of and in fairness to his constituents, I will give some response on behalf of the Minister.
The Hon. Member continues to express concern over the employment levels at Transcona, in spite of reassurances by the Minister and CN. CN has made it clear that Transcona is and will continue to be a vital facility for the railway. CN is investing to improve the facility. For example, a $10 million expansion to the wheel repair shop is under way, and CN expects employment and work levels to grow over the long term.

The recession has, of course, had an effect on the level of traffic, and hence on the amount of maintenance. Both railways have been put in a position to have temporary layoffs, but CN has and will continue to treat all its maintenance centres in the same way. It is not CN's intention to single out one of its facilities to bear the brunt of the effects of the recession.
The Hon. Member should know that the work done for VIA Rail at Transcona is only one of the many activities there. Some adjustments to the maintenance requirements for passenger cars may be necessary. However, any change must be seen in light of CN's assurance that it will have little impact on long-term employment levels at the Transcona shop.
